## Paper

## Abstract

Tailoring the electronic or ionic conduction properties of solid-state electrolytes with precision is essential to fulfilling the functional demands of electrochemical energy storage and conversion technologies. Here, the synergistic regulation of Na+ and O2− ions conduction in the Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ conductor is achieved by the non-stoichiometric ratio strategy. Crystal structure and electrical property analyses reveal that all samples feature a Pbma orthorhombic structure. With rising Na content, the defect characteristics shift from vacancies to interstitials, the NbO 6 octahedra experience a change from being compressed to normal and then to being obliquely flattened, which leads to an expansion of the corresponding interstitials in the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks. By changing the structures of these three types of polyhedron and networks, the conduction channels of Na+ and O2− ions as well as electrons can be effectively regulated. The O2− ions are the main charge carriers for Na-deficient samples, stoichiometric samples feature the mixed O2− ions and intrinsic electrons, while Na⁺ ions become the dominant carriers for Na-excess samples. This work highlights the important role of lattice defects and oxygen octahedral distortions/twisting on the conductivity, offering insights into the design of and Na+/O2− ions migration pathways in solid-state ion conductors.

---

## Introduction

Solid-state ion conductors as a class of advanced materials have broad applications in critical technologies such as all-solid-state batteries, solid oxide fuel cells, ion membranes, sensors and other advanced devices1–7. The architectures of solid-ion conductors are predominantly classified into two categories, the fluorite structure and perovskite structure8–13. It is worth noting that the perovskite structure with the general formula ABO3 exhibits an abundance of physical properties due to its unique crystal structure and tunability. Recent endeavors in exploring perovskite-structured functional ceramics have unearthed innovative ionic conductivity, spotlighting their remarkable application promise within the realm of solid-state ionic conductors14,15.

In perovskite-structured solid-state ionic conductors, a widely adopted strategy for enhancing ionic conductivity involves hetero-valent ion substitution8–10,16–20. Hetero-valent ion doping can introduce defects such as A/B-site and O vacancies, thereby enhancing the conductivity based on the vacancy mechanism16–20. On the other hand, A/B-site vacancies with high polarizability weaken the A-O/B-O bond strength, which is beneficial for enhancing the O2− ions conductivity. Li et al. achieved an O2− ionic conductivity approaching 0.01 S cm-1 by introducing Mg2+ ions at the B-site of Bi 0.5 Na 0.5 TiO 3 (BNT)-based ionic conductors8. It is known that the significant influence of defects in perovskite structure on the electrical properties is related to the behaviors such as oxygen octahedral distortion and torsion21–23. The symmetries of the perovskite-related lattice are key characteristics of oxygen octahedral distortion, tilting, and ordering, all of which are crucial parameters for improving ionic conductivity. Experiments on Ti doping of NaNbO 3 conducted by Gouget et al. provided compelling evidence for the significant influence of Nb(Ti)O 6 polyhedral deformation on ionic conductivity24. Since hetero-valent ion-modified NaNbO 3 perovskite typically involves two types of charge carriers, namely A-site cations and oxygen anions. A new question arises regarding the correspondence between the forms of oxygen octahedral deformation and the two types of charge carriers. In an effort to analyze this issue, many research works have analyzed the conductivity mechanism of NaNbO 3-based ceramics. NaNbO 3-based ceramics undergo abundant phase transitions and NbO 6 octahedral distortions in response to the variations in temperature and defect configurations. In the framework of the NaNbO 3 crystal structure, it is clear that O2− ions can migrate via the internal pathways of NbO 6 octahedra8,22,25,26. This implies a strong correlation between the variations in O2− ion channels and the inherent distortion of NbO 6 octahedra, which resonates with the proposition of Gouget and colleagues that elongated or flattened Nb(Ti)O 6 octahedra facilitate oxygen migration21. In contrast, lattice Na⁺ ions traverse the channels formed by the O atoms at the vertices of four NbO 6 octahedra, while interstitial Na⁺ ions may rely on the channels formed by the interstices of the Na-O-Na or Na-O-Nb networks27–29. There is a close connection between the changes in the Na+ ions channels and those caused by the distortion and torsion behaviors of the NbO 6 octahedra. The related perspective that Na+ ions pass through a triangular region formed by three O atoms, which is considered to be the bottleneck for Na⁺ ion diffusion, has been confirmed in the NaSICON-type materials30–32. Drawing on the understanding outlined above, elucidating the correlations between lattice defects, the distortion and torsional patterns of NbO 6 octahedra, and charge carriers in solid-state ionic conductors is of considerable significance for the defect-mediated modulation of electrical conductivity.

Here, the CaZrO 3 modified NaNbO 3 (Na 0.96 Ca 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3) solid-state ionic conductor with a perovskite structure is employed as the research subject, and the physical mechanism of its conductivity was analyzed. This doping strategy effectively stabilizes the antiferroelectric Pbma phase, ensuring that Na0.96Ca0.04Nb0.96Zr0.04O3 adopts a single-phase structure at the onset and maintains its intrinsic electrical conductivity. Synergistic modulation of Na+ and O2− ions conduction in the Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ (NCNZ-Nax, x=0.96-1.02) ceramics was successfully achieved by adjusting the non-stoichiometric ratio strategy. Crystal structure and electrical property analyses reveal that both stoichiometric and non-stoichiometric samples feature a Pbma orthorhombic structure. As Na content increases, defects transform from vacancies to interstitials. The NbO 6 octahedra undergo a change from being compressed to normal and then to being twisted and flattened, which leads to the expansion of the corresponding interstices of Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks. The synergistic interaction between the flattened NbO 6 octahedra and oxygen vacancies serves as a critical determinant in the formation of O2− ion channels. Meanwhile, the expansion of the corresponding interstices of Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks effectively enlarges the bottleneck for the migration of Na+ ions, thereby facilitating the establishment of Na+ ion channels, as depicted in schematic Fig. 1. Through the regulation of these channels, a coordinated control of the Na+/O2− ionic conductors is achieved. This work provides insights into the formation of Na+ and O2− ion migration channels in solid-state ion conductors.

---

## Results

Phase and microstructure analysis
Figure 2 shows the XRD patterns of the NCNZ-Nax samples, all samples exhibit the same pure perovskite structure, and there is no diffraction peak of a second phase. This is consistent with the uniform grain distribution observed in the SEM/TEM images with no abnormal second-phase grains (Figs. S1 and S2). The only change is that as the Na content increases, the grain size grows. Significantly, a shift towards a lower angle is observed for NCNZ-Nax samples with increasing Na content in the expanded XRD pattern (Fig. S3). For the Na-deficient samples, both Na-vacancies and oxygen vacancies generated to maintain the charge balance can cause lattice shrinkage33–35. In case of excess Na, the excess Na enters the lattice interstice and causes the crystal lattice expansion. Similar phenomena were also found in the non-stoichiometric BNT-based ceramics14,15. In order to further understand the evolution of lattice parameters with variation of Na content, GSAS software was used to refine the XRD data36,37. It is found that the use of orthorhombic phase (Pbma) for refinement can obtain better refinement results (Fig. 2b), and the lattice constant a and c and gradually increase with the increase of Na content (Tables S1 and S2).

The refined data were imported into Diamond software to observe the local environment of the atoms. Due to the low number of O vacancies (V O••) and Na vacancies (V'Na) in the compound, it is impossible to accurately identify oxygen and Na sites that are partially occupied. The unit cell of the Pbma phase, as shown in Fig. S4, is composed of two symmetric parts (a−b−c− and a−b−c+), and the a−b−c− structural part is selected for analysis in Fig. 2c. The local environments of Nb5+ and Na+ ions for NCNZ-Na 0.96, NCNZ-Na 1.0 and NCNZ-Na 1.02 samples are shown in Fig. 2c and Fig. S5. For the Na-deficient samples, the average bond distances (~1.9940 Å) for d(Nb-O3) and d(Nb-O4) in the equatorial plane are shorter than those in the stoichiometric samples (~1.9941 Å), and there is a large difference between these bond distances and those in the stoichiometric samples. Meanwhile, d(Nb-O1) and d(Nb-O2) bond distances also decrease relatively, and the change in d(Nb-O2) is more significant. The phenomenon suggests the emergence of flattened NbO 6 octahedra21,25,26. In comparison to the Na-excess (NCNZ-Na 1.02) sample, a reduction is also observed in the bond distances d(Nb-O4), while an increase is noted in the bond distances d(Nb-O3). Concurrently, a decrease in both d(Nb-O1) and d(Nb-O2) is detected. The change in the equatorial plane is characterized primarily by increased asymmetry. The decrease in the distance d(Nb-O1/O2) between the apical oxygen atoms is in contrast to the increase in the unit-cell parameters. This finding unveils a substantial distortion and torsion within the NbO 6 octahedra, which in turn triggers alterations in the unit-cell parameters. Besides, the alteration of NbO 6 octahedra also leads to the expansion of the interstitial spaces within the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks (Fig. S6). Upon increasing the Na content from 1.0 to 1.02, notable changes in the cross-sectional interstitial distances were observed. In the Na-O-Na network, the d(Na-Na) distance increases from 3.894 Å to 3.896 Å, and the d(O-O) distance increases from 4.482 Å to 4.489 Å. The d(Na-Na) spacing varies modestly, whereas the NbO 6 octahedra change substantially, suggesting a strong correlation between unit-cell volume fluctuations and NbO 6 octahedra characteristics. In the Na-O-Nb network, the d(Na-Nb) distance grows from 3.378 Å to 3.379 Å, and the d(O-O) distance increases from 2.800 Å to 2.810 Å (Fig. S6). The expansion of the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks serves to diminish the migration energy barrier for Na+ ions. Under the influence of Na stoichiometry ratios, NbO 6 octahedra, Na-O-Na, and Na-O-Nb networks are tilted and flattened, leading to changes in O2−/Na+ ionic channels.

The atomic-scale microstructure of the NCNZ-Nax samples was examined along the [110] axis using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) (Fig. 3a–h). The atomic images were processed via Fourier transform and geometric phase analysis (GPA) to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the structure and strain distribution. All samples have an orthorhombic structure (Fig. 3a and e), the interplanar spacings of 3.84 Å and 3.85 Å correspond to the (040) crystal planes, and the interplanar spacing of 3.91 Å is related to the (101) planes. Compared with NCNZ-Na 1.0 sample, the distribution of A-site vacancies is represented by the occurrence of significant intensity variations between neighboring columns of atoms in the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample34,38–41. The relatively weaker sites, which represent Na-vacancies, are marked with red triangles in Fig. 3c. The increase in atomic spacing along the [040] crystal direction in Fig. 3b compared to that in Fig. 3f also confirms the lattice strain phenomenon caused by the presence of Na-vacancies. Clearly, the GPA of NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample shows a stronger strain distribution along the xx and yy directions (Fig. 3d). In the strain mapping, the color change from dark blue to green and from orange to bright yellow represents compressive and tensile strains, respectively. The stronger tensile strain in the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample is attributed to the presence of Na-vacancies, which cause significant lattice unit deformation. Due to the significant difference in nuclear charge values, it is difficult to identify the atomic columns of O-sites in HR-TEM images (Figs. 3b and 3f). Consequently, XPS was utilized to comprehensively analyze the surface chemical composition and variation of O-vacancies of the NCNZ-Nax ceramics. The O1s peak is deconvoluted into two distinct components, denoted as peak O1 and peak O2 (Fig. 3i–k). The O1 peak centered at approximately 529.5 eV can be ascribed to lattice oxygen, whereas the peak O2 at around 531.5 eV corresponded to oxygen vacancies34,42. A notable trend is observed: the concentration of oxygen vacancies increases markedly with decreasing Na content. In the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample, the substantial presence of oxygen vacancies can be attributed to the generation of positively-charged oxygen vacancies to counterbalance the negatively-charged vacancies resulting from the Na-deficiency. Therefore, combining the above HR-TEM and XPS results, it is known that the synergistic effect between cation vacancies (V'Na) and oxygen vacancies (V O••) leads to significant lattice distortion.

Electrical performance analysis
Temperature dependent XRD patterns (Fig. 4a) directly reveal the phase transition behavior in the NCNZ-Nax samples. It is observed that the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample transitions from orthorhombic (Pbma, Pnmm, Ccmm) to tetragonal (P4/mbm) and then to cubic (Pm-3m) phases from room temperature to 700 °C. Unit-cell symmetry and volume changes are related to NbO 6 octahedra distortion and torsion. Besides, the temperature-dependent dielectric constant and loss are presented in Fig. 4b–g. In the temperature range from 300 °C to 600 °C, the NCNZ-Nax samples display two distinct phase transition peaks, corresponding to the transitions from the orthorhombic antiferroelectric Pbma (P) phase to the orthorhombic ferroelectric Pnmm (R) phase, and the tetragonal P4/mbm (T 2) phase to the cubic Pm-3m (U) phase, respectively43,44. Prominently, intense phase transition peaks of T 2-U (~560 °C) are observed in the NCNZ-Nax samples with increasing Na-deficiency (Fig. 4b–d). The formation of vacancies caused by Na-deficiency results in significant lattice contraction and oxygen octahedral distortion. These vacancies are highly susceptible to temperature variations, with significant changes in oxygen octahedral and unit-cell parameters as the temperature increases, thereby giving rise to distinct phase transition peaks. Differently, the characteristics of the T 2-U phase transition are further attenuated with increasing Na content (Fig. 4f and g). This is because interstitial Na+ ions compensate for lattice expansion caused by temperature increase. However, as the temperature increases, the interstitial Na+ ions are thermally activated and a more pronounced behavior of increased dielectric loss is observed in the T 2-U phase transition region (Fig. 4f and g).

Impedance spectroscopy tests were performed to investigate the conductance behavior of the NCNZ-Nax samples. However, the equivalent circuit modeling does not ensure correspondence between the electrical components and the underlying complex processes during spectral analysis. Also, it represents the global response at the cell level rather than representing the electrical transport phenomena at each component. The contributions from these distinct processes are buried in the impedance spectroscopy response. Therefore, the distribution of relaxation time (DRT) and the electrochemical characterization of the symmetrical (ECS) are combined for analysis, and a good fit is obtained. The DRT method reveals the dominant relaxations and their corresponding resistances as bounded by the log f axis and the distribution function. These resistances are inserted as constants in the modified ECS. Then the fitting dependencies are simulated to correctly describe the impedance data, and theoretical details can be found in the Supporting Information45–50. An example of such a fitting combined with detailed fragmentation of the spectra is given in Fig. 5a. Peaks with similar frequencies and lower intensities corresponding to DRT are regarded as RC (Resistor-Capacitance circuit) units, and the characteristic capacitance value C is fitted using Zview based on the capacitance value relationship formula (Eq. 1)51.

C = 1 / (2πf max R) (1)

As shown in Fig. 5a, the first semicircle corresponds to the grain effect of NCNZ-Nax ceramics. The characteristic capacitance value is 2.2458×10-11 F·cm-1 and the frequency at the maximum value of the semicircle is 1.06×106 Hz, which proves this statement. The second semicircle is composed of two arcs, each corresponding to an RC element. The characteristic capacitance of the first arc is 1.6990×10-10 F·cm-1 and the characteristic capacitance of the second arc is 1.3857×10-10 F·cm-1. Both of these arcs are attributed to the grain boundary effect, which is consistent with the result of the C’ spectra (Fig. S7b). Temperature-dependent capacitances of grain and grain boundary (Fig. S8) align well with the dielectric spectra (Fig. 4b–g). Notably, the capacitance of grain boundary is approximately 5×10-10 F·cm-1 and exhibit temperature independent, whereas the capacitance of grain decreases significantly as temperature increases (Fig. S8). The last polarization tail consists of four parts that can be classified into two categories. One with characteristic capacitances ranges from 3.9537×10-7 to 9.0655×10-7 F·cm⁻¹ and frequencies from 2860 to 274 Hz. The other with characteristic capacitances spans from 1.4754×10-6 to 1.3352×10-6 F·cm⁻¹ and frequencies from 42.8 to 8.7 Hz. The former category is associated with the ohmic contact resistance at the electrolyte/electrode interface or the high relaxation steps of the electrode fabrication process. In contrast, the latter category is ascribed to the electrode level, given its relatively larger capacitance and lower frequency. As depicted in Fig. 5b, a notable trend is observed that the impedance diminishes with the increment of Na-sites non-stoichiometry. This phenomenon strongly suggests that an augmentation of Na-site defects can effectively facilitate the ionic conductivity. In the DRT analysis (Fig. 5c), an intriguing behavior of the response peaks is revealed. As the Na content rises, the grain boundary response peak undergoes a significant shift. A jump movement towards a higher index occurs between the NCNZ-Na 1.0 and NCNZ-Na 1.01 samples. In contrast, the grain response peaks remain relatively stable, showing no significant alteration. These findings provide compelling evidence that the charge carriers in the solid-state ionic conductor are predominantly ions, and their characteristics are closely correlated with the varying Na content. When there is either a deficiency or an excess of Na, different distortion and torsion modes of the NbO 6 octahedra, in combination with Na-site defects and O-vacancies, collectively contribute to the observed behavior. This synergy not only influences the type of charge carriers (mainly O2− and Na+ ions), but also shapes the overall ionic conductivity of the NCNZ-Nax ceramics.

As the temperature rises, the resistance decreases for the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample (Fig. 5d). This is attributed to the fact that at higher temperatures, a greater number of carriers can surmount the energy barriers and move freely. The same phenomenon is also observed in the impedance spectra of NCNZ-Na 1.0 and NCNZ-Na 1.02 samples (Fig. S9). Significantly, notable alterations of DRT profiles are observed in both the peak relaxation times (τ) and areas of the grain boundary response peaks with τ of 10-3 s to 10-5 s as the temperature ascends (Fig. 5f and Fig. S7a). The variation in the τ peaks serves as an indicator of the changes in the electrical response, whereas the peak area corresponds to the impedance of the associated process. By extracting the τ associated with the grain boundary relaxation peak and applying the Arrhenius equation for fitting, the activation energy (E a) can be determined 1.24 eV for the NCNZ-Na 1.0 samples (Fig. S10). The relaxation peak corresponds to a unique relaxation process within the conductor, and its associated relaxation time serves as the energy barrier that must be overcome during the conductance process. Interestingly, it can be observed that the τ of grain boundaries shifts towards higher index direction with increasing temperature for the NCNZ-Na 0.96 samples (Fig. 5e). The variation of grain relaxation time is similar to that of grain boundaries, and the response peak disappears above 540 °C (Fig. 5f). When correlated with the dielectric temperature spectra in Fig. 4, the temperature interval of 540°C–560°C aligns precisely with the position of the phase transition peak from the tetragonal phase T 2 to the cubic phase U.

To determine the changes in the dominant charge carriers as a function of Na content and temperature, impedance spectroscopy measurements under flowing nitrogen, air, and oxygen atmospheres were conducted52–54. As illustrated in Fig. 6a–c, all samples exhibit characteristic Warburg behavior, indicative of ionic conduction55. The transition from nitrogen to air to oxygen reflects a progressive increase in oxygen partial pressure. Notably, the significant variation in impedance observed in Fig. 6a and b with increasing oxygen partial pressure suggests a shift in the dominant charge carriers within the ceramics. Given that under an oxygen atmosphere, the conductivity is mainly attributed to O2− ions, while the Na⁺ ion conductivity is suppressed. In contrast, under a nitrogen atmosphere, it is evident that the NCNZ-Na 0.96 and NCNZ-Na 1.0 ceramics exhibit a mixed conductivity mode of Na+/e− based on their intrinsic properties. Subsequently, the total ionic conductivity is calculated by obtaining the resistance from the intercept of the semicircle with the x-coordinate (Fig. S11). The activation energy (E a) is evaluated using the Arrhenius method,

σ = σ 0 exp(−Ea / kT) (2)

Here, T denotes the temperature in Kelvin, and k stands for the Boltzmann constant23. The results of the calculations are depicted in Fig. 6d–f and Fig. S10. The consistency between the activation energy from fitting τ and σ shows the rationality and effectiveness of the DRT transformation analysis.

In the Arrhenius plots of NCNZ-Na 0.96 (Fig. 6d), a distinct relationship between σ values, oxygen partial pressure, and temperature is revealed. When the temperature is ≤540°C, a decrement in oxygen partial pressure leads to the highest σ value under a nitrogen atmosphere. Intriguingly, the σ values in air and oxygen environments are indistinguishable, strongly suggesting that O2− ions serve as the primary charge carriers in air, while the conduction of Na⁺ ions is effectively inhibited. At temperatures ≥560°C, the highest σ is observed in an oxygen-rich atmosphere. The σ values in air and nitrogen are comparable, with slightly higher ones under nitrogen. The E a decreases significantly in air and oxygen environments, and the transition point of E a precisely corresponds to the T 2-U phase transition of the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample (Fig. 4b). This correlation indicates that the phase transition exerts a profound influence on E a, and the cubic U phase is highly favorable for O2− ions conduction. The shift of DRT peaks to higher indices in Fig. 5f offers further insights. It indicates a lower relaxation time and higher frequency, which is favorable for ion conduction. The Arrhenius plot of the NCNZ-Na 1.0 sample is presented in Fig. 6e. As the oxygen partial pressure decreases, the σ value under nitrogen is the highest, while the σ values under oxygen and air are observed to be the same, indicating that O2− ions and Na+ ions are the charge carriers in air and oxygen atmospheres. In a nitrogen atmosphere, the charge carriers are Na+ ions and e−. At 560 °C, the evidence of the charge carriers is observed. By comparing the Eₐ and σ values of the NCNZ-Na 0.96 and NCNZ-Na 1.0 samples, it finds that as the Na-deficiency increases, the σ values of O2− ions under oxygen and air atmospheres increase by nearly 100 times, which is much higher than the increase in the σ values of O2−/e− under a nitrogen atmosphere. Combined with the XRD analysis results, it is shown that the distortion and torsion modes of the NbO 6 octahedra under Na-deficient conditions are more favorable for O2− ions conduction. In addition, the Arrhenius plot of the NCNZ-Na 1.02 sample (Fig. 6f) shows a significant overall increase in σ under the condition of Na-excess, while the value of E a changes little under various atmospheres. The overlaps of the σ-T curves and impedance spectra (Fig. 6c) between the different atmospheres in the NCNZ-Na 1.02 samples allow us to determine that it is not the O2− ions that are responsible for the conductivity. Obviously, the E a values are not segmented over the entire temperature range and in different atmospheres. This is due to the fact that the excess sodium lead to lattice expansion, which makes the phase transitions smoother (Fig. 4g).

To delve deeper into the conductivity mechanism of NCNZ-Nax samples, a sandwich structure was devised. 8YSZ (8% yttria-stabilized zirconia) was employed to block Na+ ion conduction, thereby enabling a precise study of O2− ion transport24. The structure is illustrated in Fig. 7a and Fig. S12, depicting a sandwiched configuration. SEM images reveal that the sandwiched sample has a dense, homogeneous microstructure. The distinct compositional boundaries are observed at the interfaces between layers, suggesting no interdiffusion of elements. The observed homogeneous interfaces are conducive to O2− ions mobility. To quantitatively assess the contributions of Na+ and O2− ion conductivities, Eqs. 3 and 4 are employed to separately calculate their respective proportions of conductivity24,

t O2− = σ O2− / (σ Na+ + σ O2− + σ e−) = σ O2− / σ total (3)

t Na+ = σ Na+ / (σ Na+ + σ O2− + σ e−) = σ Na+ / σ total (4)

Here t quantifies the contribution of an individual ion to the total conductivity. The Na+ ion mobility can be determined by subtracting the O2− ion mobility from the total ionic mobility. Due to the small contribution of electronic conductivity, it is ignored here and the calculation process can be found in Fig. S13. Subsequent impedance spectroscopy analysis is conducted with varying Na content as shown in Fig. 7b–d.

Illustrated in Fig. 7b and c are the impedance spectra for NCNZ-Na 0.96 and NCNZ-Na 1.0, respectively. Notably, the impedance spectra for the sandwich pellet lack a polarization tail; a discrepancy is possibly attributed to variations in the low-frequency responses of yttria-stabilized zirconia and NCNZ-Nax at the electrode-electrolyte interface. The concordance of impedance spectra substantiates the validity of scrutinizing the conductivity mechanism and lends credence to the accuracy of the analytical outcomes. Furthermore, Fig. 7d reveals that the NCNZ-Na 1.02 sample manifests markedly diminished semicircles relative to the sandwich pellet, suggesting that the O2− ion conductivity is markedly inferior to the total conductivity. Utilizing Eqs. 3 and 4, the calculated values for the respective proportions of conductivity are t O2− = 8% and t Na+ = 92%. These results indicate that the charge carriers in NCNZ-Na 1.02 are Na+ ions. The curves of O2− and Na+ ions conductivity as a function of Na content (Fig. 7e) reveal that the conductivity modes can be classified into three types with the variation of Na content. They are O2− ions conductivity under Na-deficient conditions, the mixed O2− and e− conductivity at the stoichiometric component, and the Na+ ions conductivity under the presence of an excess of Na. Combined with the results of XRD analysis, the shrinkage of the equatorial plane and apical atoms of the NbO 6 octahedra, induced by sodium vacancies (V'Na) and oxygen vacancies (V••O) under Na-deficient conditions, leads to the formation of flattened NbO 6 octahedra (Fig. 2c). The structural change can lower the energy barrier for O2− ion conduction, thereby enhancing the O2− ion conductivity. Differently, when Na is in excess, the interstitial Na+ ions cause the equatorial plane of the NbO 6 octahedra to become flatter, the apical atoms to elongate, as well as leading to the expansion of the interstitial spaces within the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks (Fig. 7f, Fig. S6, and Table S3). For the Na-O-Na network, the d(Na-Na) distance expands from 3.894 Å to 3.896 Å, and the d(O-O) distance increases from 4.482 Å to 4.489 Å for the NCNZ-Na 1.02 compared to the stoichiometric component. Similarly, the d(Na-O) distance increases from 3.046 Å to 3.233 Å in the Na-O-Nb network (Fig. 7f). This expansion of the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks serves to diminish the Na+ ion migration energy barrier, leading to a significant increase in Na+ ion conductivity. Under the Na-site non-stoichiometric ratio strategy, the NbO 6 octahedra, Na-O-Na, and Na-O-Nb networks are tilted and elongated, leading to changes in the O2−/Na+ ion channels, which result in synergistic regulation of the ionic conductivity in the NaNbO 3-based solid-state ionic conductor.

In this work, the synergistic regulation of Na+/O2− ionic conduction was effectively achieved in the Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ solid-state ionic conductor by employing an A-site non-stoichiometric strategy. The correlation between the torsion and distortion patterns of NbO 6 octahedra and the conduction behavior of Na+ and O2− ions was elucidated. With rising Na content, the defect transformed from vacancies to interstitials. The NbO 6 octahedra underwent a change from flat to normal and then to twisted and flattened, which led to the expansion of the corresponding interstices of Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks. The conduction channels of Na+ and O2− ions could be effectively regulated by the changes in the NbO 6, Na-O-Na, and Na-O-Nb polyhedral structures. Given this promising insight, a comprehensive re-evaluation of other perovskite-type materials is imperative, which provides guidance for designing and optimizing functional materials with tailored ionic and electronic transport properties.

## Methods

Preparation of ceramics
Polycrystalline ceramics of Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ (abbreviated as NCNZ-Nax, x=0.96, 0.98, 0.99, 1, 1.01, and 1.02) were prepared by a traditional solid-state reaction. Carbonate, Na2CO3 (99.8%), and CaCO3 (99.8%), and oxide, Nb2O5 (99.9%), and ZrO2 (99.99%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd., CN, and used without further purification. The raw materials were dried in an oven at 180 °C for 8 h before weighing to reduce hygroscopic carbonates. Accurately weigh these reagents according to the molar ratio, and suspend them in ethanol, and then mill in a planetary ball mill for 12 h using zirconia balls. The following calcination was conducted in a covered alumina crucible at 850 °C for 2 h. To guarantee a homogeneous distribution, the calcined powders were ball-milled again for 12 h. The prepared powders have been uniaxially compacted into pellets (diameter 12 mm) with a pressure of ca. 25 MPa and pressed cold isostatically at 200 MPa. Finally, the pressed NCNZ-Nax pellets were covered with the same composition powders and then sintered at 1250~1350 °C for 2 h at a heating rate of 3 °C/min.

Characterization of ceramics
XRD patterns were recorded with a laboratory X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 ADVANCE, Bruker, Germany) using Cu Kα incident radiation (λ=1.54056 Å). Surface micromorphology, energy dispersive spectra (EDS), and selected area electron diffraction patterns (SAED) were investigated using HR-TEM (Talos F200X, FEI, USA) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (Nova NanoSEM 450, FEI, USA). Surface elemental states were studied by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Axis Ultra DLD, Shimadzu, Japan).

Electrical performance of ceramics
The working electrodes were manufactured by coating and sintering electronic paste. After sanding both sides of the ceramic sample to a flat surface, the sample was ultrasonically cleaned several times with ethanol. Then, Ag or Pt electronic paste was coated on both sides of the samples and cast at room temperature. Finally, the prepared electrodes were sintered at 850 °C for 15 min. The dielectric properties were tested in the temperature range from 25 °C~700 °C at different frequencies by using an LCR meter (Agilent E4980A, Agilent, Santa Clara, CA). AC impedance spectroscopy (IS) measurements were performed in different atmospheres (O2, air, and N2) by using an electrochemical workstation (CHI700e, CH Instruments Inc., China).

## Paper

## Abstract

Tailoring the electronic or ionic conduction properties of solid-state electrolytes with precision is essential to fulfilling the functional demands of electrochemical energy storage and conversion technologies. Here, the synergistic regulation of Na+ and O2− ions conduction in the Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ conductor is achieved by the non-stoichiometric ratio strategy. Crystal structure and electrical property analyses reveal that all samples feature a Pbma orthorhombic structure. With rising Na content, the defect characteristics shift from vacancies to interstitials, the NbO 6 octahedra experience a change from being compressed to normal and then to being obliquely flattened, which leads to an expansion of the corresponding interstitials in the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks. By changing the structures of these three types of polyhedron and networks, the conduction channels of Na+ and O2− ions as well as electrons can be effectively regulated. The O2− ions are the main charge carriers for Na-deficient samples, stoichiometric samples feature the mixed O2− ions and intrinsic electrons, while Na⁺ ions become the dominant carriers for Na-excess samples. This work highlights the important role of lattice defects and oxygen octahedral distortions/twisting on the conductivity, offering insights into the design of and Na+/O2− ions migration pathways in solid-state ion conductors.

---

## Introduction

Solid-state ion conductors as a class of advanced materials have broad applications in critical technologies such as all-solid-state batteries, solid oxide fuel cells, ion membranes, sensors and other advanced devices1–7. The architectures of solid-ion conductors are predominantly classified into two categories, the fluorite structure and perovskite structure8–13. It is worth noting that the perovskite structure with the general formula ABO3 exhibits an abundance of physical properties due to its unique crystal structure and tunability. Recent endeavors in exploring perovskite-structured functional ceramics have unearthed innovative ionic conductivity, spotlighting their remarkable application promise within the realm of solid-state ionic conductors14,15.

In perovskite-structured solid-state ionic conductors, a widely adopted strategy for enhancing ionic conductivity involves hetero-valent ion substitution8–10,16–20. Hetero-valent ion doping can introduce defects such as A/B-site and O vacancies, thereby enhancing the conductivity based on the vacancy mechanism16–20. On the other hand, A/B-site vacancies with high polarizability weaken the A-O/B-O bond strength, which is beneficial for enhancing the O2− ions conductivity. Li et al. achieved an O2− ionic conductivity approaching 0.01 S cm-1 by introducing Mg2+ ions at the B-site of Bi 0.5 Na 0.5 TiO 3 (BNT)-based ionic conductors8. It is known that the significant influence of defects in perovskite structure on the electrical properties is related to the behaviors such as oxygen octahedral distortion and torsion21–23. The symmetries of the perovskite-related lattice are key characteristics of oxygen octahedral distortion, tilting, and ordering, all of which are crucial parameters for improving ionic conductivity. Experiments on Ti doping of NaNbO 3 conducted by Gouget et al. provided compelling evidence for the significant influence of Nb(Ti)O 6 polyhedral deformation on ionic conductivity24. Since hetero-valent ion-modified NaNbO 3 perovskite typically involves two types of charge carriers, namely A-site cations and oxygen anions. A new question arises regarding the correspondence between the forms of oxygen octahedral deformation and the two types of charge carriers. In an effort to analyze this issue, many research works have analyzed the conductivity mechanism of NaNbO 3-based ceramics. NaNbO 3-based ceramics undergo abundant phase transitions and NbO 6 octahedral distortions in response to the variations in temperature and defect configurations. In the framework of the NaNbO 3 crystal structure, it is clear that O2− ions can migrate via the internal pathways of NbO 6 octahedra8,22,25,26. This implies a strong correlation between the variations in O2− ion channels and the inherent distortion of NbO 6 octahedra, which resonates with the proposition of Gouget and colleagues that elongated or flattened Nb(Ti)O 6 octahedra facilitate oxygen migration21. In contrast, lattice Na⁺ ions traverse the channels formed by the O atoms at the vertices of four NbO 6 octahedra, while interstitial Na⁺ ions may rely on the channels formed by the interstices of the Na-O-Na or Na-O-Nb networks27–29. There is a close connection between the changes in the Na+ ions channels and those caused by the distortion and torsion behaviors of the NbO 6 octahedra. The related perspective that Na+ ions pass through a triangular region formed by three O atoms, which is considered to be the bottleneck for Na⁺ ion diffusion, has been confirmed in the NaSICON-type materials30–32. Drawing on the understanding outlined above, elucidating the correlations between lattice defects, the distortion and torsional patterns of NbO 6 octahedra, and charge carriers in solid-state ionic conductors is of considerable significance for the defect-mediated modulation of electrical conductivity.

Here, the CaZrO 3 modified NaNbO 3 (Na 0.96 Ca 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3) solid-state ionic conductor with a perovskite structure is employed as the research subject, and the physical mechanism of its conductivity was analyzed. This doping strategy effectively stabilizes the antiferroelectric Pbma phase, ensuring that Na0.96Ca0.04Nb0.96Zr0.04O3 adopts a single-phase structure at the onset and maintains its intrinsic electrical conductivity. Synergistic modulation of Na+ and O2− ions conduction in the Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ (NCNZ-Nax, x=0.96-1.02) ceramics was successfully achieved by adjusting the non-stoichiometric ratio strategy. Crystal structure and electrical property analyses reveal that both stoichiometric and non-stoichiometric samples feature a Pbma orthorhombic structure. As Na content increases, defects transform from vacancies to interstitials. The NbO 6 octahedra undergo a change from being compressed to normal and then to being twisted and flattened, which leads to the expansion of the corresponding interstices of Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks. The synergistic interaction between the flattened NbO 6 octahedra and oxygen vacancies serves as a critical determinant in the formation of O2− ion channels. Meanwhile, the expansion of the corresponding interstices of Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks effectively enlarges the bottleneck for the migration of Na+ ions, thereby facilitating the establishment of Na+ ion channels, as depicted in schematic Fig. 1. Through the regulation of these channels, a coordinated control of the Na+/O2− ionic conductors is achieved. This work provides insights into the formation of Na+ and O2− ion migration channels in solid-state ion conductors.

---

## Results

Phase and microstructure analysis
Figure 2 shows the XRD patterns of the NCNZ-Nax samples, all samples exhibit the same pure perovskite structure, and there is no diffraction peak of a second phase. This is consistent with the uniform grain distribution observed in the SEM/TEM images with no abnormal second-phase grains (Figs. S1 and S2). The only change is that as the Na content increases, the grain size grows. Significantly, a shift towards a lower angle is observed for NCNZ-Nax samples with increasing Na content in the expanded XRD pattern (Fig. S3). For the Na-deficient samples, both Na-vacancies and oxygen vacancies generated to maintain the charge balance can cause lattice shrinkage33–35. In case of excess Na, the excess Na enters the lattice interstice and causes the crystal lattice expansion. Similar phenomena were also found in the non-stoichiometric BNT-based ceramics14,15. In order to further understand the evolution of lattice parameters with variation of Na content, GSAS software was used to refine the XRD data36,37. It is found that the use of orthorhombic phase (Pbma) for refinement can obtain better refinement results (Fig. 2b), and the lattice constant a and c and gradually increase with the increase of Na content (Tables S1 and S2).

The refined data were imported into Diamond software to observe the local environment of the atoms. Due to the low number of O vacancies (V O••) and Na vacancies (V'Na) in the compound, it is impossible to accurately identify oxygen and Na sites that are partially occupied. The unit cell of the Pbma phase, as shown in Fig. S4, is composed of two symmetric parts (a−b−c− and a−b−c+), and the a−b−c− structural part is selected for analysis in Fig. 2c. The local environments of Nb5+ and Na+ ions for NCNZ-Na 0.96, NCNZ-Na 1.0 and NCNZ-Na 1.02 samples are shown in Fig. 2c and Fig. S5. For the Na-deficient samples, the average bond distances (~1.9940 Å) for d(Nb-O3) and d(Nb-O4) in the equatorial plane are shorter than those in the stoichiometric samples (~1.9941 Å), and there is a large difference between these bond distances and those in the stoichiometric samples. Meanwhile, d(Nb-O1) and d(Nb-O2) bond distances also decrease relatively, and the change in d(Nb-O2) is more significant. The phenomenon suggests the emergence of flattened NbO 6 octahedra21,25,26. In comparison to the Na-excess (NCNZ-Na 1.02) sample, a reduction is also observed in the bond distances d(Nb-O4), while an increase is noted in the bond distances d(Nb-O3). Concurrently, a decrease in both d(Nb-O1) and d(Nb-O2) is detected. The change in the equatorial plane is characterized primarily by increased asymmetry. The decrease in the distance d(Nb-O1/O2) between the apical oxygen atoms is in contrast to the increase in the unit-cell parameters. This finding unveils a substantial distortion and torsion within the NbO 6 octahedra, which in turn triggers alterations in the unit-cell parameters. Besides, the alteration of NbO 6 octahedra also leads to the expansion of the interstitial spaces within the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks (Fig. S6). Upon increasing the Na content from 1.0 to 1.02, notable changes in the cross-sectional interstitial distances were observed. In the Na-O-Na network, the d(Na-Na) distance increases from 3.894 Å to 3.896 Å, and the d(O-O) distance increases from 4.482 Å to 4.489 Å. The d(Na-Na) spacing varies modestly, whereas the NbO 6 octahedra change substantially, suggesting a strong correlation between unit-cell volume fluctuations and NbO 6 octahedra characteristics. In the Na-O-Nb network, the d(Na-Nb) distance grows from 3.378 Å to 3.379 Å, and the d(O-O) distance increases from 2.800 Å to 2.810 Å (Fig. S6). The expansion of the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks serves to diminish the migration energy barrier for Na+ ions. Under the influence of Na stoichiometry ratios, NbO 6 octahedra, Na-O-Na, and Na-O-Nb networks are tilted and flattened, leading to changes in O2−/Na+ ionic channels.

The atomic-scale microstructure of the NCNZ-Nax samples was examined along the [110] axis using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) (Fig. 3a–h). The atomic images were processed via Fourier transform and geometric phase analysis (GPA) to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the structure and strain distribution. All samples have an orthorhombic structure (Fig. 3a and e), the interplanar spacings of 3.84 Å and 3.85 Å correspond to the (040) crystal planes, and the interplanar spacing of 3.91 Å is related to the (101) planes. Compared with NCNZ-Na 1.0 sample, the distribution of A-site vacancies is represented by the occurrence of significant intensity variations between neighboring columns of atoms in the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample34,38–41. The relatively weaker sites, which represent Na-vacancies, are marked with red triangles in Fig. 3c. The increase in atomic spacing along the [040] crystal direction in Fig. 3b compared to that in Fig. 3f also confirms the lattice strain phenomenon caused by the presence of Na-vacancies. Clearly, the GPA of NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample shows a stronger strain distribution along the xx and yy directions (Fig. 3d). In the strain mapping, the color change from dark blue to green and from orange to bright yellow represents compressive and tensile strains, respectively. The stronger tensile strain in the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample is attributed to the presence of Na-vacancies, which cause significant lattice unit deformation. Due to the significant difference in nuclear charge values, it is difficult to identify the atomic columns of O-sites in HR-TEM images (Figs. 3b and 3f). Consequently, XPS was utilized to comprehensively analyze the surface chemical composition and variation of O-vacancies of the NCNZ-Nax ceramics. The O1s peak is deconvoluted into two distinct components, denoted as peak O1 and peak O2 (Fig. 3i–k). The O1 peak centered at approximately 529.5 eV can be ascribed to lattice oxygen, whereas the peak O2 at around 531.5 eV corresponded to oxygen vacancies34,42. A notable trend is observed: the concentration of oxygen vacancies increases markedly with decreasing Na content. In the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample, the substantial presence of oxygen vacancies can be attributed to the generation of positively-charged oxygen vacancies to counterbalance the negatively-charged vacancies resulting from the Na-deficiency. Therefore, combining the above HR-TEM and XPS results, it is known that the synergistic effect between cation vacancies (V'Na) and oxygen vacancies (V O••) leads to significant lattice distortion.

Electrical performance analysis
Temperature dependent XRD patterns (Fig. 4a) directly reveal the phase transition behavior in the NCNZ-Nax samples. It is observed that the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample transitions from orthorhombic (Pbma, Pnmm, Ccmm) to tetragonal (P4/mbm) and then to cubic (Pm-3m) phases from room temperature to 700 °C. Unit-cell symmetry and volume changes are related to NbO 6 octahedra distortion and torsion. Besides, the temperature-dependent dielectric constant and loss are presented in Fig. 4b–g. In the temperature range from 300 °C to 600 °C, the NCNZ-Nax samples display two distinct phase transition peaks, corresponding to the transitions from the orthorhombic antiferroelectric Pbma (P) phase to the orthorhombic ferroelectric Pnmm (R) phase, and the tetragonal P4/mbm (T 2) phase to the cubic Pm-3m (U) phase, respectively43,44. Prominently, intense phase transition peaks of T 2-U (~560 °C) are observed in the NCNZ-Nax samples with increasing Na-deficiency (Fig. 4b–d). The formation of vacancies caused by Na-deficiency results in significant lattice contraction and oxygen octahedral distortion. These vacancies are highly susceptible to temperature variations, with significant changes in oxygen octahedral and unit-cell parameters as the temperature increases, thereby giving rise to distinct phase transition peaks. Differently, the characteristics of the T 2-U phase transition are further attenuated with increasing Na content (Fig. 4f and g). This is because interstitial Na+ ions compensate for lattice expansion caused by temperature increase. However, as the temperature increases, the interstitial Na+ ions are thermally activated and a more pronounced behavior of increased dielectric loss is observed in the T 2-U phase transition region (Fig. 4f and g).

Impedance spectroscopy tests were performed to investigate the conductance behavior of the NCNZ-Nax samples. However, the equivalent circuit modeling does not ensure correspondence between the electrical components and the underlying complex processes during spectral analysis. Also, it represents the global response at the cell level rather than representing the electrical transport phenomena at each component. The contributions from these distinct processes are buried in the impedance spectroscopy response. Therefore, the distribution of relaxation time (DRT) and the electrochemical characterization of the symmetrical (ECS) are combined for analysis, and a good fit is obtained. The DRT method reveals the dominant relaxations and their corresponding resistances as bounded by the log f axis and the distribution function. These resistances are inserted as constants in the modified ECS. Then the fitting dependencies are simulated to correctly describe the impedance data, and theoretical details can be found in the Supporting Information45–50. An example of such a fitting combined with detailed fragmentation of the spectra is given in Fig. 5a. Peaks with similar frequencies and lower intensities corresponding to DRT are regarded as RC (Resistor-Capacitance circuit) units, and the characteristic capacitance value C is fitted using Zview based on the capacitance value relationship formula (Eq. 1)51.

C = 1 / (2πf max R) (1)

As shown in Fig. 5a, the first semicircle corresponds to the grain effect of NCNZ-Nax ceramics. The characteristic capacitance value is 2.2458×10-11 F·cm-1 and the frequency at the maximum value of the semicircle is 1.06×106 Hz, which proves this statement. The second semicircle is composed of two arcs, each corresponding to an RC element. The characteristic capacitance of the first arc is 1.6990×10-10 F·cm-1 and the characteristic capacitance of the second arc is 1.3857×10-10 F·cm-1. Both of these arcs are attributed to the grain boundary effect, which is consistent with the result of the C’ spectra (Fig. S7b). Temperature-dependent capacitances of grain and grain boundary (Fig. S8) align well with the dielectric spectra (Fig. 4b–g). Notably, the capacitance of grain boundary is approximately 5×10-10 F·cm-1 and exhibit temperature independent, whereas the capacitance of grain decreases significantly as temperature increases (Fig. S8). The last polarization tail consists of four parts that can be classified into two categories. One with characteristic capacitances ranges from 3.9537×10-7 to 9.0655×10-7 F·cm⁻¹ and frequencies from 2860 to 274 Hz. The other with characteristic capacitances spans from 1.4754×10-6 to 1.3352×10-6 F·cm⁻¹ and frequencies from 42.8 to 8.7 Hz. The former category is associated with the ohmic contact resistance at the electrolyte/electrode interface or the high relaxation steps of the electrode fabrication process. In contrast, the latter category is ascribed to the electrode level, given its relatively larger capacitance and lower frequency. As depicted in Fig. 5b, a notable trend is observed that the impedance diminishes with the increment of Na-sites non-stoichiometry. This phenomenon strongly suggests that an augmentation of Na-site defects can effectively facilitate the ionic conductivity. In the DRT analysis (Fig. 5c), an intriguing behavior of the response peaks is revealed. As the Na content rises, the grain boundary response peak undergoes a significant shift. A jump movement towards a higher index occurs between the NCNZ-Na 1.0 and NCNZ-Na 1.01 samples. In contrast, the grain response peaks remain relatively stable, showing no significant alteration. These findings provide compelling evidence that the charge carriers in the solid-state ionic conductor are predominantly ions, and their characteristics are closely correlated with the varying Na content. When there is either a deficiency or an excess of Na, different distortion and torsion modes of the NbO 6 octahedra, in combination with Na-site defects and O-vacancies, collectively contribute to the observed behavior. This synergy not only influences the type of charge carriers (mainly O2− and Na+ ions), but also shapes the overall ionic conductivity of the NCNZ-Nax ceramics.

As the temperature rises, the resistance decreases for the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample (Fig. 5d). This is attributed to the fact that at higher temperatures, a greater number of carriers can surmount the energy barriers and move freely. The same phenomenon is also observed in the impedance spectra of NCNZ-Na 1.0 and NCNZ-Na 1.02 samples (Fig. S9). Significantly, notable alterations of DRT profiles are observed in both the peak relaxation times (τ) and areas of the grain boundary response peaks with τ of 10-3 s to 10-5 s as the temperature ascends (Fig. 5f and Fig. S7a). The variation in the τ peaks serves as an indicator of the changes in the electrical response, whereas the peak area corresponds to the impedance of the associated process. By extracting the τ associated with the grain boundary relaxation peak and applying the Arrhenius equation for fitting, the activation energy (E a) can be determined 1.24 eV for the NCNZ-Na 1.0 samples (Fig. S10). The relaxation peak corresponds to a unique relaxation process within the conductor, and its associated relaxation time serves as the energy barrier that must be overcome during the conductance process. Interestingly, it can be observed that the τ of grain boundaries shifts towards higher index direction with increasing temperature for the NCNZ-Na 0.96 samples (Fig. 5e). The variation of grain relaxation time is similar to that of grain boundaries, and the response peak disappears above 540 °C (Fig. 5f). When correlated with the dielectric temperature spectra in Fig. 4, the temperature interval of 540°C–560°C aligns precisely with the position of the phase transition peak from the tetragonal phase T 2 to the cubic phase U.

To determine the changes in the dominant charge carriers as a function of Na content and temperature, impedance spectroscopy measurements under flowing nitrogen, air, and oxygen atmospheres were conducted52–54. As illustrated in Fig. 6a–c, all samples exhibit characteristic Warburg behavior, indicative of ionic conduction55. The transition from nitrogen to air to oxygen reflects a progressive increase in oxygen partial pressure. Notably, the significant variation in impedance observed in Fig. 6a and b with increasing oxygen partial pressure suggests a shift in the dominant charge carriers within the ceramics. Given that under an oxygen atmosphere, the conductivity is mainly attributed to O2− ions, while the Na⁺ ion conductivity is suppressed. In contrast, under a nitrogen atmosphere, it is evident that the NCNZ-Na 0.96 and NCNZ-Na 1.0 ceramics exhibit a mixed conductivity mode of Na+/e− based on their intrinsic properties. Subsequently, the total ionic conductivity is calculated by obtaining the resistance from the intercept of the semicircle with the x-coordinate (Fig. S11). The activation energy (E a) is evaluated using the Arrhenius method,

σ = σ 0 exp(−Ea / kT) (2)

Here, T denotes the temperature in Kelvin, and k stands for the Boltzmann constant23. The results of the calculations are depicted in Fig. 6d–f and Fig. S10. When the temperature is ≤540°C, a decrement in oxygen partial pressure leads to the highest σ value under a nitrogen atmosphere. Intriguingly, the σ values in air and oxygen environments are indistinguishable, strongly suggesting that O2− ions serve as the primary charge carriers in air, while the conduction of Na⁺ ions is effectively inhibited. At temperatures ≥560°C, the highest σ is observed in an oxygen-rich atmosphere. The σ values in air and nitrogen are comparable, with slightly higher ones under nitrogen. The E a decreases significantly in air and oxygen environments, and the transition point of E a precisely corresponds to the T 2-U phase transition of the NCNZ-Na 0.96 sample (Fig. 4b). This correlation indicates that the phase transition exerts a profound influence on E a, and the cubic U phase is highly favorable for O2− ions conduction. The shift of DRT peaks to higher indices in Fig. 5f offers further insights. It indicates a lower relaxation time and higher frequency, which is favorable for ion conduction. The Arrhenius plot of the NCNZ-Na 1.0 sample is presented in Fig. 6e. As the oxygen partial pressure decreases, the σ value under nitrogen is the highest, while the σ values under oxygen and air are observed to be the same, indicating that O2− ions and Na+ ions are the charge carriers in air and oxygen atmospheres. In a nitrogen atmosphere, the charge carriers are Na+ ions and e−. At 560 °C, the evidence of the charge carriers is observed. By comparing the Eₐ and σ values of the NCNZ-Na 0.96 and NCNZ-Na 1.0 samples, it finds that as the Na-deficiency increases, the σ values of O2− ions under oxygen and air atmospheres increase by nearly 100 times, which is much higher than the increase in the σ values of O2−/e− under a nitrogen atmosphere. Combined with the XRD analysis results, it is shown that the distortion and torsion modes of the NbO 6 octahedra under Na-deficient conditions are more favorable for O2− ions conduction. In addition, the Arrhenius plot of the NCNZ-Na 1.02 sample (Fig. 6f) shows a significant overall increase in σ under the condition of Na-excess, while the value of E a changes little under various atmospheres. The overlaps of the σ-T curves and impedance spectra (Fig. 6c) between the different atmospheres in the NCNZ-Na 1.02 samples allow us to determine that it is not the O2− ions that are responsible for the conductivity. Obviously, the E a values are not segmented over the entire temperature range and in different atmospheres. This is due to the fact that the excess sodium lead to lattice expansion, which makes the phase transitions smoother (Fig. 4g).

To delve deeper into the conductivity mechanism of NCNZ-Nax samples, a sandwich structure was devised. 8YSZ (8% yttria-stabilized zirconia) was employed to block Na+ ion conduction, thereby enabling a precise study of O2− ion transport24. The structure is illustrated in Fig. 7a and Fig. S12, depicting a sandwiched configuration. SEM images reveal that the sandwiched sample has a dense, homogeneous microstructure. The distinct compositional boundaries are observed at the interfaces between layers, suggesting no interdiffusion of elements. The observed homogeneous interfaces are conducive to O2− ions mobility. To quantitatively assess the contributions of Na+ and O2− ion conductivities, Eqs. 3 and 4 are employed to separately calculate their respective proportions of conductivity24,

t O2− = σ O2− / (σ Na+ + σ O2− + σ e−) = σ O2− / σ total (3)

t Na+ = σ Na+ / (σ Na+ + σ O2− + σ e−) = σ Na+ / σ total (4)

Here t quantifies the contribution of an individual ion to the total conductivity. The Na+ ion mobility can be determined by subtracting the O2− ion mobility from the total ionic mobility. Due to the small contribution of electronic conductivity, it is ignored here and the calculation process can be found in Fig. S13. Subsequent impedance spectroscopy analysis is conducted with varying Na content as shown in Fig. 7b–d.

Illustrated in Fig. 7b and c are the impedance spectra for NCNZ-Na 0.96 and NCNZ-Na 1.0, respectively. Notably, the impedance spectra for the sandwich pellet lack a polarization tail; a discrepancy is possibly attributed to variations in the low-frequency responses of yttria-stabilized zirconia and NCNZ-Nax at the electrode-electrolyte interface. The concordance of impedance spectra substantiates the validity of scrutinizing the conductivity mechanism and lends credence to the accuracy of the analytical outcomes. Furthermore, Fig. 7d reveals that the NCNZ-Na 1.02 sample manifests markedly diminished semicircles relative to the sandwich pellet, suggesting that the O2− ion conductivity is markedly inferior to the total conductivity. Utilizing Eqs. 3 and 4, the calculated values for the respective proportions of conductivity are t O2− = 8% and t Na+ = 92%. These results indicate that the charge carriers in NCNZ-Na 1.02 are Na+ ions. The curves of O2− and Na+ ions conductivity as a function of Na content (Fig. 7e) reveal that the conductivity modes can be classified into three types with the variation of Na content. They are O2− ions conductivity under Na-deficient conditions, the mixed O2− and e− conductivity at the stoichiometric component, and the Na+ ions conductivity under the presence of an excess of Na. Combined with the results of XRD analysis, the shrinkage of the equatorial plane and apical atoms of the NbO 6 octahedra, induced by sodium vacancies (V'Na) and oxygen vacancies (V••O) under Na-deficient conditions, leads to the formation of flattened NbO 6 octahedra (Fig. 2c). The structural change can lower the energy barrier for O2− ion conduction, thereby enhancing the O2− ion conductivity. Differently, when Na is in excess, the interstitial Na+ ions cause the equatorial plane of the NbO 6 octahedra to become flatter, the apical atoms to elongate, as well as leading to the expansion of the interstitial spaces within the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks (Fig. 7f, Fig. S6, and Table S3). For the Na-O-Na network, the d(Na-Na) distance expands from 3.894 Å to 3.896 Å, and the d(O-O) distance increases from 4.482 Å to 4.489 Å for the NCNZ-Na 1.02 compared to the stoichiometric component. Similarly, the d(Na-O) distance increases from 3.046 Å to 3.233 Å in the Na-O-Nb network (Fig. 7f). This expansion of the Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks serves to diminish the Na+ ion migration energy barrier, leading to a significant increase in Na+ ion conductivity. Under the Na-site non-stoichiometric ratio strategy, the NbO 6 octahedra, Na-O-Na, and Na-O-Nb networks are tilted and elongated, leading to changes in the O2−/Na+ ion channels, which result in synergistic regulation of the ionic conductivity in the NaNbO 3-based solid-state ionic conductor.

In this work, the synergistic regulation of Na+/O2− ionic conduction was effectively achieved in the Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ solid-state ionic conductor by employing an A-site non-stoichiometric strategy. The correlation between the torsion and distortion patterns of NbO 6 octahedra and the conduction behavior of Na+ and O2− ions was elucidated. With rising Na content, the defect transformed from vacancies to interstitials. The NbO 6 octahedra underwent a change from flat to normal and then to twisted and flattened, which led to the expansion of the corresponding interstices of Na-O-Na and Na-O-Nb networks. The conduction channels of Na+ and O2− ions could be effectively regulated by the changes in the NbO 6, Na-O-Na, and Na-O-Nb polyhedral structures. Given this promising insight, a comprehensive re-evaluation of other perovskite-type materials is imperative, which provides guidance for designing and optimizing functional materials with tailored ionic and electronic transport properties.

## Methods

Preparation of ceramics
Polycrystalline ceramics of Na 0.96xCa 0.04 Nb 0.96 Zr 0.04 O 3-δ (abbreviated as NCNZ-Nax, x=0.96, 0.98, 0.99, 1, 1.01, and 1.02) were prepared by a traditional solid-state reaction. Carbonate, Na2CO3 (99.8%), and CaCO3 (99.8%), and oxide, Nb2O5 (99.9%), and ZrO2 (99.99%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd., CN, and used without further purification. The raw materials were dried in an oven at 180 °C for 8 h before weighing to reduce hygroscopic carbonates. Accurately weigh these reagents according to the molar ratio, and suspend them in ethanol, and then mill in a planetary ball mill for 12 h using zirconia balls. The following calcination was conducted in a covered alumina crucible at 850 °C for 2 h. To guarantee a homogeneous distribution, the calcined powders were ball-milled again for 12 h. The prepared powders have been uniaxially compacted into pellets (diameter 12 mm) with a pressure of ca. 25 MPa and pressed cold isostatically at 200 MPa. Finally, the pressed NCNZ-Nax pellets were covered with the same composition powders and then sintered at 1250~1350 °C for 2 h at a heating rate of 3 °C/min.

Characterization of ceramics
XRD patterns were recorded with a laboratory X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 ADVANCE, Bruker, Germany) using Cu Kα incident radiation (λ=1.54056 Å). Surface micromorphology, energy dispersive spectra (EDS), and selected area electron diffraction patterns (SAED) were investigated using HR-TEM (Talos F200X, FEI, USA) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (Nova NanoSEM 450, FEI, USA). Surface elemental states were studied by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Axis Ultra DLD, Shimadzu, Japan).

Electrical performance of ceramics
The working electrodes were manufactured by coating and sintering electronic paste. After sanding both sides of the ceramic sample to a flat surface, the sample was ultrasonically cleaned several times with ethanol. Then, Ag or Pt electronic paste was coated on both sides of the samples and cast at room temperature. Finally, the prepared electrodes were sintered at 850 °C for 15 min. The dielectric properties were tested in the temperature range from 25 °C~700 °C at different frequencies by using an LCR meter (Agilent E4980A, Agilent, Santa Clara, CA). AC impedance spectroscopy (IS) measurements were performed in different atmospheres (O2, air, and N2) by using an electrochemical workstation (CHI700e, CH Instruments Inc., China).

The exploration of the conductance behavior of perovskite solid-state ionic
conductors is carried out through Nyquist curve analysis. The electrochemical response
process from high frequency to low frequency includes responses from the bulk phase,
grain boundaries, electrodes, etc. Currently, the main analysis method is to perform
equivalent circuit fitting using Zview software. Nevertheless, some of the
electrochemical response Nyquist semicircles highly overlap, making it impossible to
determine the number of CP elements in the equivalent circuit, which will affect the
19

distribution of relaxation times (DRT). The equivalent circuit model related to the
electrochemical process is accurately measured, and the test results are specifically
